kurz: The remaining federal tax breaks for retirement savers: the Saver's Credit, the health savings account, plans for the self-employed, Roth conversions and the backdoor Roth, with the rules for 2026.

bloecke.md:
The IRA and the 401(k) are the main tax-advantaged accounts, but not the only ones. The tax code offers a credit for savers with low incomes, a health account that can double as a retirement account, plans for the self-employed with much higher limits, and ways to move money from pre-tax to Roth. Each tool has its own rules, and several of them change in 2026 and 2027.

Federal support for retirement saving works almost entirely through deductions and exclusions, whose value grows with the tax rate. The one exception aimed at low incomes is the Saver's Credit, which will be replaced by a matching contribution, the Saver's Match, from 2027. The information in this lesson reflects the situation in October 2026.

bloecke.md:
## The Saver's Credit

The retirement savings contributions credit, usually called the Saver's Credit, rewards contributions to an IRA, a 401(k), a 403(b), a 457(b), a SIMPLE IRA or an ABLE account (26 U.S.C. § 25B). It amounts to 50%, 20% or 10% of up to $2,000 of contributions per person, depending on adjusted gross income. Spouses filing jointly can each claim it. You must be at least 18, not a full-time student and not claimed as a dependent on someone else's return. Distributions from retirement accounts in the two previous years and up to the filing deadline reduce the eligible contributions.

The credit is nonrefundable. It can reduce your federal income tax to zero, but no further. Many of the people with the lowest incomes owe little or no income tax and therefore receive less than the headline rate. It is claimed on Form 8880.

bloecke.beispiel: A single filer with an AGI of $22,000 contributes $2,000 to a Roth IRA. The rate is 50%, so the credit would be $1,000. After the standard deduction of $16,100, taxable income is $5,900 and the tax is $590. The credit is therefore limited to $590, which is still 29.5% of the contribution.

bloecke.md: Under SECURE 2.0, the Saver's Credit is replaced for tax years from 2027 by the Saver's Match. The federal government then pays a matching contribution of 50% of up to $2,000 of contributions per person, at most $1,000, directly into the saver's IRA or workplace plan instead of reducing the tax bill. The match phases out over an income range set in the law, for joint filers from $41,000 to $71,000, with the ranges indexed to inflation after 2027. Because the money is deposited even if no income tax is owed, the match reaches savers whom the nonrefundable credit missed. Withdrawals of the matched money are taxable. The Treasury Department is still working on the procedures.

## The health savings account

A health savings account (HSA) is the only account with a triple tax advantage: contributions are deductible or excluded from pay, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free (26 U.S.C. § 223). To contribute, you must be covered by an HSA-eligible high-deductible health plan, with a minimum deductible of $1,700 for self-only and $3,400 for family coverage in 2026, and have no other disqualifying coverage. Since 2026, bronze and catastrophic plans from the health insurance marketplace also qualify.

In 2026, you can contribute $4,400 with self-only coverage and $8,750 with family coverage, plus $1,000 from age 55. Contributions through payroll are also free of Social Security and Medicare tax, which no other retirement account offers. The money stays yours when you change jobs and can be invested in funds. Contributions end when you enroll in Medicare.

A family in the 22% bracket contributes the full $8,750 through payroll. It saves $1,925 in federal income tax and $669.38 in Social Security and Medicare tax, $2,594.38 in total. California and New Jersey do not follow the federal rules and tax HSA contributions.

Anyone who can pay current medical costs from other money can leave the HSA invested. $4,400 a year at a return of 5% grows to around $145,500 in 20 years. Medical expenses incurred after the HSA was opened can be reimbursed tax-free years later, as long as you keep the receipts. From age 65, withdrawals for other purposes are taxed as ordinary income like those from a Traditional IRA, without the 20% additional tax that applies before 65.

## Self-employed: SEP IRA and Solo 401(k)

Self-employed people have no employer plan, but they can set up their own. With a **SEP IRA** (simplified employee pension), the business contributes up to 25% of pay. For a sole proprietor, this works out to 20% of net self-employment earnings after deducting half of the self-employment tax. The maximum is $72,000 in 2026. A SEP can be set up and funded until the tax filing deadline including extensions. If the business has eligible employees, it must contribute the same percentage of pay for them.

A **Solo 401(k)** is available if the business has no employees other than the owner and a spouse. The owner contributes twice: as employee, up to $24,500 of deferrals in 2026, plus catch-up contributions from 50; and as employer, the same 20% of net earnings as with a SEP. Together, the contributions excluding catch-ups may not exceed $72,000. At low and middle profits, the Solo 401(k) therefore allows much more. It can also include a Roth option. Once plan assets exceed $250,000, an annual Form 5500-EZ is required. For businesses with up to 100 employees, the SIMPLE IRA is a third option with lower limits and mandatory employer contributions.

- The employee deferral limit of $24,500 applies per person across all plans. If you also defer in an employer's 401(k), less remains for the Solo 401(k).
- A Solo 401(k) is no longer possible once you hire employees who meet the eligibility rules; the plan must then be converted or opened to them.
- The calculation in the table is simplified. Wages from another job, the qualified business income deduction or a business structured as an S corporation change the result.
- A pre-tax SEP or SIMPLE IRA counts towards the pro-rata rule for a backdoor Roth; a Solo 401(k) does not.

## Roth conversions

You can convert money from a Traditional IRA or a pre-tax 401(k) to a Roth account at any time and at any income. The converted amount, minus any basis, is taxable as ordinary income in the year of the conversion. The 10% additional tax does not apply to the conversion itself, but if you are under 59½, each conversion has its own five-year period before the converted amount can be withdrawn without the additional tax. Since 2018, a conversion can no longer be undone.

A conversion pays off when the tax rate today is lower than the expected rate on later withdrawals. The years between retirement and the start of Social Security and required distributions are often such a window. Converting $20,000 in the 12% bracket costs $2,400 of tax now, after which the money and its growth stay tax-free. Watch the side effects: the conversion raises income for premium tax credits on marketplace health insurance and, two years later, for Medicare premiums.

## The backdoor Roth

People whose income is above the Roth IRA limits can still get money into a Roth IRA in two steps. They make a nondeductible contribution to a Traditional IRA and then convert it to a Roth IRA. If there is no other pre-tax IRA money, the conversion is almost tax-free, because only the small growth between the two steps is taxed. Both steps are reported on Form 8606.

The obstacle is the pro-rata rule. For tax purposes, all your Traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs count as one account, valued on 31 December of the year of the conversion, with the amounts converted during the year added back. Each conversion carries the same share of basis as the combined balance. Money in a 401(k) does not count. Some 401(k) plans also allow after-tax contributions beyond the $24,500 deferral limit up to the total limit of $72,000, with an in-plan conversion to Roth. This is called the mega backdoor Roth and depends entirely on the plan.

An investor contributes $7,500 to a Traditional IRA without a deduction and converts it to a Roth IRA. She also has a rollover IRA with $67,500 of pre-tax money from an earlier 401(k).

- Balance of all Traditional IRAs on 31 December ($67,500) plus the amount converted ($7,500): $75,000, of which $7,500 is basis, that is 10%.
- Of the $7,500 converted, only 10% is tax-free; $6,750 is taxable as ordinary income.
- The remaining basis of $6,750 stays in the Traditional IRA and is tracked on Form 8606.

If her current employer's 401(k) accepts incoming rollovers, she can move the $67,500 into it before the end of the year. The conversion is then almost entirely tax-free.

## Other routes into a Roth account

Since 2024, beneficiaries of a 529 college savings plan can move unused money to a Roth IRA in their own name, up to $35,000 over their lifetime (SECURE 2.0). The 529 account must have existed for at least 15 years, contributions from the last five years and their earnings are excluded, and each year's rollover counts towards the annual IRA limit and requires compensation. Employees of state and local governments can use a governmental 457(b) in addition to a 403(b), because the two have separate limits; withdrawals after leaving the job are free of the 10% additional tax.

- The Treasury Department has not yet completed all procedures for the Saver's Match from 2027, for example how the deposit reaches the account.
- For Trump accounts, the Treasury and the IRS are still issuing guidance; details of the investments and of employer contributions may still change.
- Contribution limits, income ranges and credit thresholds are adjusted for inflation each year. The figures in this lesson apply to 2026.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of July 2025 created Trump accounts, a type of IRA for children under 18. Since 4 July 2026, parents, relatives and others can contribute up to $5,000 a year in total; employers can contribute up to $2,500 a year tax-free for an employee's child, counted within that limit. For children who are US citizens and born from 2025 to 2028, the federal government deposits a one-time $1,000 if an election is made. The money must be invested in low-cost funds that track a US stock index. Contributions are not deductible, and growth is tax-deferred. Withdrawals are not possible before the year in which the child turns 18; after that, the account largely follows the rules of a Traditional IRA. Details of the procedures are still being issued.

- Check your adjusted gross income against the Saver's Credit table. Contributing pre-tax to a 401(k) can move you into a higher credit rate.
- If your health plan qualifies for an HSA, contribute through payroll to also save Social Security and Medicare tax, and keep receipts for medical expenses.
- As a self-employed person, compare the SEP IRA and the Solo 401(k) well before year end; the deadlines for setting up the plan and for making each type of contribution differ, so check them with the provider.
- Before a backdoor Roth, add up all Traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRA balances. Without a plan for the pro-rata rule, the conversion can become largely taxable.
- Plan Roth conversions together with Medicare premiums and marketplace subsidies, not in isolation.

Beyond the IRA and 401(k), the Saver's Credit rewards low incomes with up to 50% of the first $2,000, the HSA offers the only triple tax advantage, and self-employed people can shelter up to $72,000 a year. Roth conversions shift tax from later to now; whether that pays off depends on the tax rate in the year of conversion compared with the rate on later withdrawals.

Account for people with an HSA-eligible high-deductible health plan. Contributions are deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free; from 65, other withdrawals are taxed like those from a Traditional IRA.

Simplified employee pension; an IRA into which a self-employed person or small employer contributes up to 25% of pay, at most $72,000 in 2026. For sole proprietors, the limit works out to about 20% of net self-employment earnings.

401(k) for a business without employees other than the owner and a spouse. The owner can contribute as employee (up to $24,500 in 2026 plus catch-up) and as employer (about 20% of net earnings), up to $72,000 in total excluding catch-ups.

Transfer of pre-tax money from a Traditional IRA or plan to a Roth account. The converted amount, minus basis, is taxable as ordinary income in the year of conversion; since 2018, a conversion cannot be undone.

Rule under which all Traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs of a person count as one account for the taxation of distributions and conversions. Each conversion contains the same share of basis as the combined balance on 31 December.
